title: Animals matter
hookLine: Jewish law requires feeding your animals before yourself (Berakhot 40a)
last: WAGES BEFORE SUNDOWN; WORK WITH ALL YOUR STRENGTH.

cards: Six-thirty in the morning. The coffee is brewing, your stomach is complaining, and the cat is sitting by the bowl, staring. Who eats first?
It sounds like a question of manners, or of who complains loudest. The Talmud treats it as a question of law.
In tractate Berakhot, the teacher Rav Yehudah says, in Rav's name, that a person may not eat until they have fed their animals. So the cat's breakfast comes before yours.

teach.h: GRASS FOR THE CATTLE, THEN YOU EAT.
teach.b: First, the order of a verse. The rule comes from a line in Deuteronomy, read as part of the Shema: "And I will give grass in thy fields for thy cattle, and thou shalt eat and be satisfied."
The rabbis noticed the order: the cattle are given grass, and then you eat. They made the verse's order into the household's order. Second, the Torah's other rules.
Don't muzzle an ox while it treads out the grain; it may eat from what it works. Rest on the Sabbath includes your ox and your donkey. If your enemy's donkey is lying under its load, help lift it.

The rabbis gathered teachings like these under a name you met in year one, tza'ar ba'alei chayim, the suffering of living things, and treated causing animals needless suffering as forbidden. Third, a story.

teach.h: A CALF HIDES IN A ROBE.
teach.b: In tractate Bava Metzia, a calf being led to slaughter runs to Rabbi Judah the Prince, hides its head in his robe, and cries. He tells it: go, for this you were created.
The Talmud says suffering came upon him for that, because he showed no compassion. One day his housekeeper is about to sweep out a litter of small animals.

teach.h: HIS MERCIES OVER ALL HIS WORKS.
teach.b: He stops her, quoting a psalm: "his tender mercies are over all his works." And the Talmud says his suffering ended. Fourth, what it means.
Jewish law permits eating meat, with rules. But in these texts an animal is never a mere thing.
Its hunger comes first at breakfast, and its fear in a doorway matters.

how: Jewish law codes rule, following Berakhot 40a, that a person feeds their animals before eating, and tza'ar ba'alei chayim is studied as a principle of Jewish law.

games.q: you're Rabbi Judah the Prince. a calf on its way to slaughter runs to you and hides its head in your robe, crying. what do you say?
o: go, for this you were created.
stay; I'll buy you from the butcher.
games.why: he says, go, for this you were created. the Talmud says suffering came upon him because he showed no compassion, and left only when he later spared small animals.

practice: If you have a pet, plan to fill its bowl before your next meal, and watch it eat.
If you don't, there's still a way: a bird feeder, a dish of water on a hot step, a neighbor's dog to greet, or simply some care with the small life around you.
Let one animal you'll meet today come to mind, notice its hunger, its tiredness, its fear, and choose one small kindness to give it before you look after yourself.

wordCard.voice: Animals matter. The rabbis' phrase is tza'ar ba'alei chayim, the suffering of living things, and they put an animal's meal before your own. Today's word.
